report:
Based on this research, here is my report:

**Conclusion: The claim is not supported — capsaicin has not been shown to "treat" breast cancer in humans.**

**What the evidence actually shows:**

1. **Cell culture (in vitro) studies**: Multiple lab studies using human breast cancer cell lines (MCF-7, BT-20, MDA-MB-231) show capsaicin can inhibit cell proliferation, induce cell-cycle arrest, and trigger apoptosis, and it may modulate EGFR/HER-2 signaling relevant to some breast cancer subtypes (https://www.spandidos-publications.com/10.3892/mmr.2020.11585, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0960327110396530, https://www.nature.com/articles/onc2009335.pdf). These are preliminary, mechanistic findings in dishes, not evidence of clinical benefit.

2. **Animal studies are mixed**: Some xenograft/rodent models suggest anti-tumor effects, but other studies found capsaicin *promotes* tumor growth in mouse skin cancer models (DMBA/TPA-induced), highlighting that effects are context- and dose-dependent, not uniformly anticancer (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25846502/).

3. **A comprehensive scientific review** concludes that "the clinical value of per os (oral) capsaicin to complement chemotherapy is still speculative," while acknowledging decent preclinical/animal evidence for effects on tumor growth and metastasis — but explicitly stopping short of clinical proof (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/).

4. **The only real human clinical trials involving capsaicin and breast cancer** are not testing it as a cancer treatment — they test topical capsaicin patches for managing **chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN)** or post-surgical nerve pain in breast cancer patients (CAPTRANE and QUCIP trials), a symptom-management use, not tumor treatment (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/18/14/2355, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11763653/).

**Bottom line**: Capsaicin shows interesting anticancer activity in lab and some animal studies, but there is no clinical trial evidence it treats breast cancer in humans. Existing human trials use it only for pain relief in cancer patients, not as an anticancer therapy. The claim as stated is premature/unsupported.
